passages.title: The first census
passages.summary: In the second year after Egypt, the LORD tells Moses to count Israel. The count covers men twenty and older who can go to war. One leader from each tribe helps Moses and Aaron. Each tribe is counted by families and fathers’ houses. The total is 603,550. The Levites are not counted with the rest. They care for the tabernacle, carry it, and camp around it. No outsider may come near it.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: How do the camp’s different duties help people support each other? The count leaves out the Levites (verse 47). What work are they given in verse 50?

contextNote.title: The census counts a defined task rather than the whole population
contextNote.text: Verse 3 counts men twenty and older “able to go out to war.” So this is a list of soldiers, not a count of everyone. Women, children, and the old are part of Israel but not of this list. The Levites are left out for a different reason (verses 47–50). Their task is the tabernacle, not the battle line. Verse 53 says their camp around the tent keeps wrath from the people. Each group is counted for the work it will do.

passages.title: The camp arranged
passages.summary: The LORD arranges the camp around the Tent of Meeting. Each tribe camps under its own banner, at a distance from the tent. Judah’s group camps on the east and sets out first. Reuben’s group camps on the south and sets out second. Then the tent moves, with the Levites in the middle. Ephraim’s group camps on the west and sets out third. Dan’s group camps on the north and sets out last. Israel camps and marches as the LORD commanded.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: The tent travels in the middle of the tribes (verse 17). What does the camp’s layout put at its center?

contextNote.title: The arrangement makes the sanctuary a shared center
contextNote.text: The chapter places three tribes on each side of the tent. The same order holds on the march. Verse 17 puts the tent and the Levites in the middle of the line. Two groups go before it, and two follow. So the tent is never at the edge, in camp or on the road. Every tribe can see where the center is from its own place. Exodus 25:8 gave the reason: God dwells among them.

passages.title: Levites and firstborn
passages.summary: Aaron’s sons Eleazar and Ithamar serve as priests after Nadab and Abihu die. The tribe of Levi is given to Aaron to help with the tabernacle. The LORD says he takes the Levites in place of every firstborn in Israel. The firstborn became his on the day he struck Egypt’s firstborn. Levite males a month old and up are counted: 22,000. Their three clans camp around the tent and each has its duties. Israel’s firstborn males number 22,273. The extra 273 are bought back at five shekels each, paid to Aaron.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: The older Church manual connects the firstborn with Israel’s escape from Egypt. The LORD takes the Levites “instead of all the firstborn” (verse 12). When did the firstborn become his (verse 13)?

contextNote.title: Levite service recalls a claim arising from the rescue
contextNote.text: Verse 13 looks back to the night of the exodus. Egypt’s firstborn died, and Israel’s firstborn were spared (Exodus 12:29; 13:2). From then on they belonged to the LORD. Verse 12 makes an exchange: one tribe serves in their place. So every Levite at work reminds Israel of that rescue. The count is exact, and 273 firstborn have no Levite to stand for them. Verses 46–48 require five shekels for each one.

passages.title: Duties for moving the sanctuary
passages.summary: The LORD orders a count of Levite men aged thirty to fifty. The sons of Kohath carry the most holy things. First Aaron and his sons cover the ark, table, lamp stand, and altars. The Kohathites must not touch or look at the holy things, or they will die. The sons of Gershon carry the curtains and coverings. The sons of Merari carry the boards, bars, pillars, and sockets. Aaron’s sons Eleazar and Ithamar direct the work. In all, 8,580 Levites are counted for this service.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: The Kohathites carry what they may not touch or see (verses 15 and 20). Who covers the holy things first?

contextNote.title: Moving sacred objects requires divisions of responsibility
contextNote.text: Moving the tent is risky work, and the chapter splits it up. The priests go in first and wrap each holy object (verses 5–14). Only then do the Kohathites come to carry the loads. Verse 15 says they must not touch the holy things “lest they die.” Verses 18–19 show concern for them: “Don’t cut off” these families. The priests’ careful covering is what keeps the carriers alive. Each group depends on another doing its part first.

passages.title: Camp, restitution, and jealousy
passages.summary: The unclean are sent outside the camp, because the LORD dwells in it. Anyone who wrongs another must confess, repay in full, and add a fifth. If no relative can receive it, the payment goes to the priest. Then comes a law for a husband who suspects his wife and has no witness. He brings her to the priest with a barley offering. The priest mixes holy water with dust from the floor, and she swears an oath. She drinks the water. If guilty, her body swells; if not, she is free and can bear children.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: What power does a husband’s accusation give him? What protection does the wife receive? Verse 14 covers a wife who “isn’t defiled.” What does verse 28 say about her?

contextNote.title: Suspicion enters a ritual with unequal household power
contextNote.text: Verse 14 names two cases under one feeling. The husband is jealous, and his wife may be guilty or innocent. There is no witness, so no court can settle it (verse 13). The law sets her “before the LORD,” not before her husband (verse 16). Only the husband can start it, and verse 31 clears him either way. Still, he may not punish her on suspicion alone. Verse 28 says an innocent wife “shall be free.”

passages.title: Nazirite vows and blessing
passages.summary: A man or woman may make a special vow as a Nazirite. For the days of the vow, the person avoids wine and anything from the grapevine. No razor touches the head, and the hair grows long. The person does not go near a dead body, even a parent’s. If someone dies nearby, the vow starts over after cleansing. When the time ends, the Nazirite brings offerings and shaves the head. Then the LORD gives the priests words to bless Israel. They ask the LORD to bless, keep, shine on, and give peace.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Verse 2 says “either man or woman” may make this vow. What three things does a Nazirite give up in verses 3–6?

contextNote.title: A special vow creates duties for a stated period
contextNote.text: Priests were born into their office, and only men of Aaron’s family held it. Verse 2 opens a different path: “either man or woman” may take this vow. The rules echo a priest’s. No wine, as for priests on duty (Leviticus 10:9). No contact with the dead, even parents, as for the high priest (Leviticus 21:11). Verse 8 gives the result: the person is “holy to the LORD.” The vow lasts for a stated time and ends with offerings (verse 13).

passages.title: Gifts from the tribal leaders
passages.summary: When the tabernacle is set up, the tribal leaders bring six wagons and twelve oxen. Moses gives two wagons to Gershon’s sons and four to Merari’s sons. Kohath’s sons get none, because they carry the holy things on their shoulders. Then each leader brings an offering for the altar, one leader each day. For twelve days every tribe gives the same gift. It is a silver platter, a silver bowl, a gold ladle of incense, and animals. The totals are listed at the end. Moses then hears the LORD’s voice from above the mercy seat.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: The wagons are shared out “according to their service” (verses 7–8). Why do Kohath’s sons get none (verse 9)?

contextNote.title: The same gift does not answer every form of work
contextNote.text: The leaders give six wagons, and Moses does not split them evenly. Gershon’s sons carry curtains and get two (verse 7; 4:25). Merari’s sons carry heavy boards and sockets and get four (verse 8; 4:31–32). Kohath’s sons carry the ark and holy things by hand, so they get none. Each group gets what its load needs. Then verses 12–83 give every tribe the same offering on its own day. So help is shared by need, and honor at the altar is shared equally.

passages.title: Levites prepared for service
passages.summary: Aaron sets the seven lamps to light the space in front of the lamp stand. The Levites are cleansed with water, shaving, and washed clothes. The whole people gather and lay hands on them. Aaron presents them to the LORD as an offering from Israel. They belong to the LORD in place of Israel’s firstborn. Then they begin their service at the tent under Aaron and his sons. A Levite serves from age twenty-five to fifty. After fifty he stops the heavy work but may still assist his brothers.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: A Levite stops the work at fifty but still assists (verses 25–26). What kinds of service fit different stages of life?

contextNote.title: Ending one duty does not end every form of service
contextNote.text: The Levites’ main work included carrying the tent and its heavy parts (chapter 4). Verses 24–25 set working years from twenty-five to fifty. Verse 26 does not send the older men home. They “assist their brothers” without doing the heavy service. So age changes the task, not the person’s place among the Levites. The people’s hands on the Levites in verse 10 show they serve for all Israel. Verse 19 calls them a gift to Aaron for the people’s sake.

passages.title: Passover and the guiding cloud
passages.summary: In the first month of the second year, Israel keeps the Passover at Sinai. Some men are unclean from touching a dead body and cannot join. They ask Moses why they must be kept back. Moses waits to hear from the LORD. The LORD says anyone unclean or far away may keep it one month later. A foreigner living with Israel may keep it by the same rules. The cloud covers the tabernacle by day and looks like fire by night. Israel camps while it rests and travels when it lifts, however long that takes.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Men who were unclean ask why they are kept back (verse 7). What answer does the LORD give in verses 10–11?

contextNote.title: A question from excluded people produces another opportunity
contextNote.text: The rule was clear: an unclean person could not eat the Passover. These men had touched a dead body (verse 6). In verse 7 they do not ask to break the rule. They ask why they should lose their place in the feast. Moses does not answer from what he already knows. He waits, and the LORD adds a second date one month later (verses 10–11). The new rule also covers travelers, and verse 13 guards it from misuse.

passages.title: Departure from Sinai
passages.summary: The LORD tells Moses to make two silver trumpets. Priests blow them to gather the people, start the march, and mark feasts. On the twentieth day of the second month the cloud lifts. Israel leaves Sinai in order, with Judah’s group first. The Levites carry the tabernacle and the holy things between the groups. Moses asks Hobab the Midianite to come and be their eyes in the wilderness. The ark goes ahead three days to find a resting place. Moses prays when the ark sets out and when it rests.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Moses asks Hobab to “be our eyes” (verse 31). Why would Moses want a guide when the cloud leads them?

contextNote.title: Divine guidance does not make human knowledge useless
contextNote.text: Israel has the cloud, the ark, and the trumpets to lead it. Yet in verse 31 Moses asks a Midianite relative for help. Hobab knows “how we are to encamp in the wilderness.” The cloud shows when and where to stop. A man who knows the wilderness can help with the camping itself. Moses does not treat these as rivals. Verse 32 promises Hobab a share in whatever good the LORD gives Israel.

passages.title: Complaints, elders, and quail
passages.summary: The people complain, and the LORD’s fire burns the edge of the camp. Then they weep for meat and remember the fish and vegetables of Egypt. They say they are tired of manna. Moses tells the LORD the burden is too heavy and asks to die. The LORD has him gather seventy elders and puts the Spirit on them. Eldad and Medad prophesy in the camp, and Moses wishes all the people were prophets. A wind brings quail, piled around the camp. While the people are still eating, a plague strikes them.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies gratitude and meekness here. Joshua wants Eldad and Medad stopped (verse 28). What does Moses wish for in verse 29?

contextNote.title: Memory changes under pressure
contextNote.text: Verse 5 gives the people’s memory of Egypt: fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, garlic. They say they ate it “for nothing.” Exodus 1:13–14 said their lives there were bitter with hard service. They ate that food as slaves. Their craving has changed what they remember. Verse 6 shows the effect: manna becomes “nothing at all.” Verse 20 names the root: they have rejected the LORD who is among them.

passages.title: Miriam and Aaron challenge Moses
passages.summary: Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses because of his Cushite wife. They ask if the LORD has spoken only through Moses. The text says Moses was very humble. The LORD calls all three to the tent and comes down in the cloud. He says he speaks to Moses plainly, mouth to mouth, not in dreams. When the cloud leaves, Miriam’s skin is leprous and white as snow. Aaron begs Moses, and Moses cries, “Heal her, God.” She is shut outside the camp seven days, and the people wait for her.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: The Church lesson studies respect for prophetic service. Moses prays for the sister who spoke against him (verse 13). What do the people do while she is outside the camp (verse 15)?

contextNote.title: The community's movement waits for an excluded member
contextNote.text: Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses, and the LORD defends him (verses 6–8). Moses himself says nothing until verse 13. His only words in the chapter are a prayer for her healing. The LORD sets a limit of seven days outside the camp. Verse 15 adds what the people did: they did not travel until she returned. The whole camp, with the cloud and the ark, waits for one person. Her correction is real, and so is her place among them.

passages.title: The spies report on Canaan
passages.summary: The LORD tells Moses to send one leader from each tribe into Canaan. Moses tells them to look at the land, the people, and the cities. They travel forty days and bring back a huge cluster of grapes. They report that the land flows with milk and honey. They also say the people are strong and the cities walled. Caleb says Israel should go up at once and is well able to win. The others say the people are too strong. They spread a bad report and say they felt like grasshoppers.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Numbers names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: The Church lesson studies Caleb’s faith. Caleb and the others saw the same land (verses 27–31). Where do their reports differ?

contextNote.title: Observation and conclusion are different parts of the report
contextNote.text: Moses asked for facts in verses 18–20: the land, the people, the cities. Verses 27–29 answer with facts, and no one disputes them. The split comes with the conclusion. Caleb says, “We are well able” (verse 30). The others say, “We aren’t able” (verse 31). Then verse 32 calls their next words “an evil report.” They now say the land eats its people and that they looked like grasshoppers.

passages.title: The people refuse to enter
passages.summary: The people weep all night and want to choose a leader and return to Egypt. Joshua and Caleb say the land is good and the LORD is with them. The people talk of stoning them. The LORD threatens to destroy them, and Moses pleads God’s name and mercy. The LORD pardons, but that generation will die in the wilderness over forty years. Only Caleb and Joshua will enter, with the children. The ten spies die of plague. The people then go up without Moses or the ark and are beaten back.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects this account with hope through faith. The people go up after being told not to (verses 41–44). What stayed in the camp?

contextNote.title: A later act does not undo the earlier refusal
contextNote.text: In verse 40 the people say, “We have sinned,” and set out to fight. It looks like the obedience they refused the day before. Moses tells them the LORD is not with them now (verses 42–43). Verse 44 says they “presumed to go up” anyway. The ark and Moses stayed in the camp. So this is a second act of not listening, not a repair of the first. Verse 45 reports the defeat that Moses had warned of.

passages.title: Offerings and reminders
passages.summary: The LORD gives rules for offerings once Israel lives in the land. Each animal offering comes with set amounts of flour, oil, and wine. The same rule applies to the foreigner living among them. The first of each batch of dough is given to the LORD. Sins done by mistake are forgiven through an offering. A person who sins with a high hand is cut off. A man found gathering sticks on the Sabbath is stoned at the LORD’s word. Israel must wear fringes with a blue cord to remember the commandments.

lds.text: How can a visible reminder help someone remember a promise? The fringe is there “that you may see it” (verse 39). What does seeing it guard against?

contextNote.title: A garment reminder reaches into ordinary acts of looking
contextNote.text: Chapter 14 showed a people led by what their eyes saw in Canaan (13:33). Verse 39 warns against following “your own heart and your own eyes.” The answer is something else to look at. A fringe with a blue cord hangs on every garment (verse 38). The order of verbs is see, remember, do. The reminder is worn all day, in ordinary work and travel. Verse 41 ties it to the exodus: the God who brought them out.

passages.title: Korah, Dathan, and Abiram rebel
passages.summary: Korah the Levite, with Dathan, Abiram, and 250 leaders, rises against Moses and Aaron. They say all the people are holy and ask why Moses lifts himself above them. Moses tells Korah’s group to bring pans of incense before the LORD. Dathan and Abiram refuse to come and accuse Moses of failing them. The ground opens and swallows the rebels’ households. Fire burns up the 250 men with their incense pans. The next day the people blame Moses and Aaron, and a plague starts. Aaron runs in with incense and stands between the dead and the living.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: The manual studies priestly authority. Korah says “all the congregation are holy” (verse 3). What does Aaron do for the people in verses 47–48?

contextNote.title: A claim about shared holiness challenges unequal duties
contextNote.text: Korah’s claim in verse 3 starts from something true. God did call all Israel a holy nation (Exodus 19:6). Korah uses it to say no one should hold a special duty. Moses hears a different aim in verse 10: Korah wants the priesthood too. The chapter then shows what the priest’s place is for. In verses 46–48 Aaron runs into the plague with incense and makes atonement. He stands “between the dead and the living,” at risk to himself.

passages.title: Aaron’s staff buds
passages.summary: The LORD tells Moses to collect a rod from the leader of each tribe. Each man’s name is written on his rod, and Aaron’s name is on Levi’s. Moses lays the twelve rods in the tent before the covenant. The rod of the man God chooses will bud. The next day Aaron’s rod has buds, blossoms, and ripe almonds. Each leader takes his own rod back. Aaron’s rod is kept in the tent as a sign against rebels. The people cry that anyone who comes near the tabernacle will die.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: How does Aaron’s flowering staff answer the dispute about leadership? Why is the rod kept (verse 10)?

contextNote.title: A retained sign answers a conflict that speech has not settled
contextNote.text: Chapter 16 ended the revolt with deaths, and the people still complained (16:41). Chapter 17 answers the same question without killing anyone. Twelve dead sticks spend a night in the tent. Only Aaron’s shows life: buds, flowers, and almonds at once (verse 8). Verse 10 says why it is kept: to end the complaints “that they not die.” So the sign is meant to protect the people. Their fear in verses 12–13 leads into the duties of chapter 18.

passages.title: Priestly duties and support
passages.summary: The LORD tells Aaron that the priests answer for the sanctuary. The Levites help them but may not touch the holy vessels or the altar. The priests receive the holy offerings, first fruits, and firstborn animals as their food. Firstborn sons and unclean animals are bought back for five shekels. Aaron gets no land, because the LORD is his portion. The Levites receive Israel’s tithe, a tenth, in return for their service. They also get no land. From the tithe they must give a tenth, the best part, to the priest.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: The Levites receive the tithe for their work (verse 21). What must they give from it in verse 26?

contextNote.title: Support for sanctuary workers creates a duty for its recipients
contextNote.text: The people ended chapter 17 afraid to go near the tent (17:13). Chapter 18 answers by naming who bears that risk. The priests and Levites do the service “that there be no more wrath” (verse 5). Verse 21 gives the Levites the tithe, since they get no land (verse 24). The gift is called pay for service, not a favor. It also brings a duty: a tenth of it goes to the priests (verse 26). Those supported by gifts are themselves givers.

passages.title: The red heifer and cleansing
passages.summary: Israel brings a red heifer, a young cow never yoked and without defect. It is killed and burned outside the camp with cedar, hyssop, and scarlet. Its ashes are stored and mixed with running water for cleansing. Anyone who touches a dead body is unclean for seven days. So is anyone in a tent of death, or who touches a bone or grave. A clean person sprinkles the water on them on the third and seventh days. Then they wash and are clean at evening. Whoever refuses the cleansing defiles the sanctuary and is cut off.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: What care do people need after a death? Touching the dead makes a person unclean seven days (verse 11). What does someone else do for that person in verses 18–19?

contextNote.title: Contact with death changes access even without deliberate wrongdoing
contextNote.text: Everyone will have to touch the dead at some time, to bury family. Verse 11 does not call this a sin. It sets a seven-day state with a fixed way out. The cleansing water is made ahead and kept ready for anyone (verse 9). A mourner cannot do the sprinkling alone. Verses 18–19 require “a clean person” to do it, on two set days. The one case that is punished is refusing the cleansing (verses 13 and 20).

passages.title: Miriam dies, water flows, and Aaron dies
passages.summary: Miriam dies at Kadesh. There is no water, and the people quarrel with Moses and Aaron. The LORD tells Moses to take the rod and speak to the rock. Moses calls the people rebels and strikes the rock twice, and water pours out. The LORD says they did not believe him and will not bring Israel in. Edom refuses to let Israel pass through, even for payment. At Mount Hor, Moses puts Aaron’s garments on his son Eleazar. Aaron dies there, and Israel weeps thirty days.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Numbers names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Moses’s choices under pressure. Moses was told to speak to the rock (verse 8). What did he say and do in verses 10–11?

contextNote.title: A long-serving leader remains subject to judgment
contextNote.text: Verse 8 told Moses to speak to the rock before the people. In verse 10 Moses speaks to the people and calls them rebels. He says “we” will bring the water, and he strikes the rock twice. The water still comes, and the people drink. Verse 12 gives God’s charge: they did not believe him or show him holy. Long service does not exempt Moses. The chapter begins with Miriam’s death and ends with Aaron’s.

passages.title: The bronze serpent and eastern victories
passages.summary: The king of Arad attacks, and Israel defeats him after a vow to the LORD. On the road around Edom the people speak against God and Moses. They call the manna disgusting food. The LORD sends venomous snakes, and many die. The people confess, and Moses prays. Moses sets a bronze snake on a pole, and whoever looks at it lives. Israel travels on and sings at a well. They defeat the kings Sihon and Og and take their land.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Numbers names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects the serpent with looking to Christ. Compare Alma 33 and Helaman 8. What did a bitten person have to do to live (verse 9)?

contextNote.title: The healing sign later becomes a question about its use
contextNote.text: The people ask Moses to pray that the snakes be taken away (verse 7). The LORD does not remove them. He gives a cure that each bitten person must use. Verse 9 states it simply: one who “looked at the serpent of bronze” lived. The cure has the shape of the thing that harmed them. Second Kings 18:4 reports that Israel later burned incense to this bronze snake. King Hezekiah broke it in pieces.

passages.title: Balak sends for Balaam
passages.summary: Israel camps in the plains of Moab, and Moab is afraid. King Balak sends for Balaam to curse Israel. God tells Balaam not to go, because the people are blessed. Balak sends higher princes and promises great honor. God lets Balaam go but only to say what God tells him. The donkey sees the LORD’s angel with a sword and turns aside three times. Balaam beats her, and the LORD opens her mouth to speak. Then Balaam sees the angel, who lets him go on with the same warning.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies how Balaam responds to pressure from the king. Who sees the angel first in verses 23–27?

contextNote.title: An outsider sees what a seer misses
contextNote.text: Balaam is hired as a man who sees and speaks for the gods (verse 6). On this road his donkey sees the angel three times, and he sees nothing. He beats her each time. The LORD opens her mouth (verse 28) and then Balaam’s eyes (verse 31). The famous seer needed both done for him. The angel says the donkey saved his life (verse 33). It prepares for chapter 23, where Balaam can say only what he is given.

passages.title: Balaam blesses Israel
passages.summary: Balaam has Balak build seven altars and offer bulls and rams. The LORD puts a word in Balaam’s mouth. Balaam asks how he can curse those whom God has not cursed. Balak takes him to a second place, where he sees only part of Israel. Seven more altars are built. Balaam says God is not a man who lies or changes his mind. God has blessed, and Balaam cannot reverse it. Balak takes him to a third place, the top of Peor.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Balak moves Balaam to a new place to get a new answer (verse 13). What does Balaam say about God in verse 19?

contextNote.title: Changing the viewpoint cannot purchase a different answer
contextNote.text: Balak’s plan in verse 13 is to change the view. From the new spot Balaam will see “just part of them.” A smaller Israel might seem easier to curse. He also repeats the full offering: seven altars, seven bulls, seven rams (verse 14). Verse 19 answers both moves. God is not a man who lies or changes his mind. Balak can move the seer, but he cannot move the one who speaks through him.

passages.title: A star and a scepter
passages.summary: Balaam sees that the LORD wants to bless Israel and uses no omens this time. The Spirit of God comes on him as he looks at Israel’s tents. He says their tents are lovely, like gardens by a river. He says those who bless Israel are blessed, and those who curse it are cursed. Balak is furious and sends him home without the promised honor. Balaam reminds him that no amount of silver could change the LORD’s word. He says a star will come from Jacob and a scepter from Israel. He speaks against Moab, Edom, Amalek, and others, and goes home.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: The Church manual connects the star and scepter with Christ. Balak says the LORD kept Balaam from honor (verse 11). How does Balaam answer in verse 13?

contextNote.title: A promised reward loses force when the message stays independent
contextNote.text: Balak hired Balaam with the promise of “great honor” (22:17). After three blessings he cancels the reward in verse 11. He even blames the LORD for the lost pay. Balaam repeats his first answer (verse 13; 22:18). A house full of silver could not change the LORD’s word. Then Balaam gives a fourth saying that no one paid for (verses 15–19). Numbers 31:16 later reports that Balaam did harm Israel by other advice.

passages.title: Peor and Phinehas
passages.summary: At Shittim, Israelite men go after Moabite women and join the sacrifices to their gods. Israel joins itself to Baal of Peor, and the LORD’s anger burns. Moses orders the judges to put the guilty to death. An Israelite man brings a Midianite woman into the camp while the people weep. Phinehas, Aaron’s grandson, kills them both with a spear. A plague stops after twenty-four thousand have died. The LORD gives Phinehas a covenant of peace and a lasting priesthood. The LORD tells Moses to treat the Midianites as enemies.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Phinehas is given “my covenant of peace” after a killing (verses 12–13). What had stopped in verse 8?

contextNote.title: A promise of peace follows a disturbing act of killing
contextNote.text: The crisis here is worship of another god, not marriage (verses 2–3). Zimri brings Cozbi past the weeping people in open view (verse 6). Phinehas kills them, and verse 8 says the plague stopped. Verses 11–13 praise him and call the act atonement. The reward is named “peace,” which sits oddly beside a spear. The text presents the killing as ending a greater loss of life. It does not hide the violence.

passages.title: The second census
passages.summary: After the plague the LORD orders a new count of men twenty and older. Moses and Eleazar count them in the plains of Moab by the Jordan. The list recalls Dathan, Abiram, and Korah, and notes that Korah’s sons did not die. It names Zelophehad’s five daughters. The total is 601,730. The land will be divided by these names: larger groups get more, smaller groups less. The place of each share is chosen by lot. No one from the first count is left except Caleb and Joshua.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Verse 64 says no one from the first count remained. Who are the two men named in verse 65?

contextNote.title: The new count organizes shares for the coming generation
contextNote.text: The first count in chapter 1 was for war. This count has a second use, stated in verse 53: dividing the land. Verse 54 sets the size of each share by the number of names. Verse 55 leaves the location to the lot. So no tribe can claim the best ground by strength. The total is nearly the same as in the first count (1:46). Verses 64–65 note that it is a new generation, as 14:29 foretold.

passages.title: The daughters’ petition and Joshua’s appointment
passages.summary: Zelophehad’s five daughters come before Moses, the priest, and the leaders. Their father died in the wilderness and left no son. They ask for land among their father’s brothers so his name is not lost. Moses brings their case to the LORD. The LORD says the daughters are right and must receive the inheritance. He makes it a rule: with no son, the land goes to a daughter. Then the LORD tells Moses he will see the land and die. Moses asks for a new leader and lays hands on Joshua before the people.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider how careful listening can reveal a gap in existing rules. The manual also studies Joshua’s appointment. What do the five daughters ask for in verse 4?

contextNote.title: A family’s case changes the rule
contextNote.text: Land was to be divided by the names of men counted in chapter 26. A man with no sons would drop out of the list. Five sisters, each named in verse 1, speak at the tent door before everyone. Verse 4 asks why their father’s name should be taken away. Moses has no ruling ready and takes the case to the LORD (verse 5). The answer is “The daughters of Zelophehad speak right.” Their case then becomes law for all Israel (verses 8–11).

passages.title: Daily, Sabbath, and festival offerings
passages.summary: The LORD tells Israel to bring his offerings at their set times. Two lambs are offered every day, one in the morning and one at evening. Each comes with flour, oil, and a drink offering. Two more lambs are offered every Sabbath. At each new month there are bulls, a ram, and seven lambs. Passover is on the fourteenth day of the first month. Seven days of unleavened bread follow, with offerings each day. The feast of weeks has its own offerings.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: The daily offering is two lambs, morning and evening (verses 3–4). How can repeated acts sustain remembrance and gratitude?

contextNote.title: A calendar creates a recurring claim on shared resources
contextNote.text: Verse 2 calls these offerings “my food,” due “in their due season.” The chapter then moves from the smallest unit of time to larger ones. Every day has two lambs (verses 3–4). Every Sabbath adds two more (verse 9). Every month and each feast add still more (verses 11 and 19). The offerings come from the whole people, not from one giver. So the calendar keeps a steady claim on Israel’s flocks and fields.

passages.title: Offerings in the seventh month
passages.summary: The seventh month has three sacred times. The first day is a day of trumpets with rest and offerings. The tenth day is a day to humble oneself and do no work. On the fifteenth day a seven-day feast begins. Thirteen bulls are offered the first day, and one fewer each day after. On the seventh day there are seven bulls. The eighth day is a solemn assembly with one bull. These offerings are in addition to vows and free gifts.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: The feast offerings drop from thirteen bulls to seven, then one (verses 13, 32, 36). How can a calendar help a community remember its duties together?

contextNote.title: The festival's pattern gives time an ordered shape
contextNote.text: The feast week has the most offerings in these two chapters. Verses 12–34 count down: thirteen bulls, then twelve, down to seven. Each day’s rams and lambs stay the same. Verse 35 marks an eighth day with a “solemn assembly” and no regular work. Its offering is small: one bull, one ram, seven lambs. So the busiest week of offerings ends in a quiet day. Verse 39 adds that all of this is apart from personal vows and gifts.

passages.title: Vows and household authority
passages.summary: Moses tells the tribal heads the LORD’s rule on vows. A man who vows must not break his word. A young woman’s vow stands if her father hears it and says nothing. If he forbids it that day, it does not stand, and the LORD forgives her. A wife’s vow stands if her husband hears and says nothing. If he forbids it that day, it is void. A widow’s or divorced woman’s vow stands. A husband who cancels a vow later bears her guilt.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Who can cancel a vow in these laws? How does that power affect family members? What does a husband’s silence do in verse 14?

contextNote.title: Silence can confirm a vow within an unequal household system
contextNote.text: Verse 2 sets the base rule: a vow must be kept. The rest deals with women under a father or husband. He may cancel her vow only on the day he hears it (verses 5, 8). Verse 14 says silence counts as consent: he “establishes” it by saying nothing. After that he cannot undo it without bearing her guilt (verse 15). So the law limits his power by a deadline. Verse 9 shows a widow or divorced woman answers for her own vows.

passages.title: War against Midian
passages.summary: The LORD tells Moses to take vengeance on Midian before he dies. Twelve thousand men go to war with Phinehas the priest. They kill Midian’s men, its five kings, and Balaam. They bring back the women, children, and herds. Moses is angry that the women were spared, because of what happened at Peor. He orders the boys and the women who have lain with a man killed. The soldiers purify themselves seven days outside the camp. The plunder is divided, and the officers give gold because no soldier was lost.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: How does war affect the families in this chapter? Whom does verse 17 name?

contextNote.title: Victory does not end the account's violence
contextNote.text: The chapter presents this war as the LORD’s answer to Peor (verses 2 and 16). The army returns as winners, and Moses meets them with anger. Verse 17 orders the killing of boys and of women who have known a man. Verse 18 keeps the young girls alive for the soldiers. The text reports these orders without softening them. It then requires every fighter to stay outside the camp and be purified (verse 19). Even a commanded war leaves those who killed unclean.

passages.title: Eastern tribes make a promise
passages.summary: Reuben and Gad have large herds and want the grazing land east of the Jordan. They ask Moses for it and ask not to cross the river. Moses asks if their brothers should go to war while they sit there. He says they are acting like the spies who discouraged Israel. They promise to build towns for their families and then fight in front of Israel. They will not go home until every tribe has its land. Moses agrees and warns that their sin will find them out if they fail. He gives them and half of Manasseh the lands of Sihon and Og.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Moses asks if their brothers should fight while they sit (verse 6). What do Reuben and Gad promise in verses 17–18?

contextNote.title: A desirable local settlement creates a question of shared burden
contextNote.text: Reuben and Gad ask for land already won, east of the river. Their last words in verse 5 are “Don’t bring us over the Jordan.” Moses hears a threat to everyone else. If two tribes stay home, the rest may lose heart, as at Kadesh. The answer is a bargain made in public. They get the land if their fighters cross and stay to the end. Their gain is allowed, but it comes with a duty to the other tribes.

passages.title: The journey remembered
passages.summary: Moses writes down the stages of Israel’s journey at the LORD’s command. The list begins at Rameses, the day after the Passover. Egypt is burying its firstborn as Israel leaves. Dozens of camps are named, from the Red Sea to Sinai to Kadesh. Aaron dies on Mount Hor in the fortieth year, at age 123. The list ends in the plains of Moab by the Jordan. The LORD tells Israel to drive out Canaan’s people and destroy their idols. Any who remain will be like thorns in Israel’s sides.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Why might a community keep a list of the places along its journey? Who wrote this list, and at whose command (verse 2)?

contextNote.title: A journey list turns movement into shared memory
contextNote.text: Verse 2 says Moses wrote these stages “by the commandment of the LORD.” So the record itself is commanded, not only the travel. Most of the entries are just two verbs: they traveled, they camped. A few stop for a memory: the Passover night, Elim’s water, Aaron’s death. The list includes the hard places with the good ones. Forty years of wandering become a line a reader can follow. It ends at the Jordan, with orders for the next step (verses 50–53).

passages.title: Borders and appointed leaders
passages.summary: The LORD gives Moses the borders of the land of Canaan. The south border runs from the Salt Sea along Edom. The Great Sea is the west border. The north and east borders are traced, ending at the Jordan and the Salt Sea. This land is for the nine and a half tribes, by lot. Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh already have land east of the Jordan. Eleazar the priest and Joshua will divide the land. One leader from each tribe is named to help, with Caleb for Judah.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: What helps people share land fairly? Verses 17–18 name who will divide it. Who are they?

contextNote.title: Dividing promised land requires named people to make decisions
contextNote.text: The first half of the chapter draws a border before any land is taken. The second half names the people who will divide it. Eleazar the priest and Joshua lead (verse 17). Verse 18 adds one leader from every tribe that will receive land. So each tribe has its own person present when shares are set. Caleb, who trusted the promise in 13:30, stands for Judah. Naming the dividers ahead of time leaves less room for dispute later.

passages.title: Levite towns and cities of refuge
passages.summary: Israel must give the Levites forty-eight towns with pasture land around them. Six of these are cities of refuge. A person who kills someone by accident may flee there from the avenger. He must not die before he stands trial before the community. One who killed with a weapon or from hatred is put to death. One who killed without hatred stays in the city until the high priest dies. No one is put to death on one witness alone. No payment can free a murderer, because blood pollutes the land.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider how fair judgment requires more than an accusation. The city protects the killer “until he stands before the congregation” (verse 12). How many witnesses does verse 30 require?

contextNote.title: Refuge delays revenge so a case can receive judgment
contextNote.text: A dead person’s relative, the “avenger of blood,” could kill the killer (verse 19). The city of refuge puts a wall between them for a time. Verse 12 gives the purpose: no death before a trial by the community. The trial asks about intent: a weapon, hatred, or lying in wait (verses 16–23). Verse 30 requires more than one witness for a death sentence. Verse 31 forbids a rich killer from paying his way out. So revenge is held back until the facts are judged.

passages.title: Inheritance and marriage
passages.summary: The family heads of Manasseh come to Moses with a problem. Zelophehad’s daughters will inherit land. If they marry men of another tribe, the land will pass to that tribe. Moses answers by the LORD’s word that they speak rightly. The daughters may marry whom they think best, but only within their father’s tribe. Any daughter who inherits land must do the same. The five daughters marry sons of their father’s brothers. So their land stays in Manasseh, and the book ends in the plains of Moab.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: How do the inheritance rules affect Zelophehad’s daughters and their choices? What two things does verse 6 say about whom they may marry?

contextNote.title: Protecting an inheritance narrows the daughters' marriage choices
contextNote.text: Chapter 27 gave the daughters their father’s land. This chapter deals with a side effect. Land followed the husband’s tribe, so their marriages could move it (verse 3). Verse 6 keeps two things together. The women choose: “whom they think best.” The choice is limited: within their father’s tribe. Their right to the land is kept, at the cost of a narrower choice.

events.title: The first census
events.summary: In the second year after Egypt, the LORD tells Moses to count Israel. The count covers men twenty and older who can go to war. One leader from each tribe helps Moses and Aaron. Each tribe is counted by families and fathers’ houses. The total is 603,550. The Levites are not counted with the rest. They care for the tabernacle, carry it, and camp around it. No outsider may come near it.
events.detail: Verse 3 counts men twenty and older “able to go out to war.” So this is a list of soldiers, not a count of everyone. Women, children, and the old are part of Israel but not of this list. The Levites are left out for a different reason (verses 47–50). Their task is the tabernacle, not the battle line. Verse 53 says their camp around the tent keeps wrath from the people. Each group is counted for the work it will do.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: How do the camp’s different duties help people support each other? The count leaves out the Levites (verse 47). What work are they given in verse 50?

events.title: The camp arranged
events.summary: The LORD arranges the camp around the Tent of Meeting. Each tribe camps under its own banner, at a distance from the tent. Judah’s group camps on the east and sets out first. Reuben’s group camps on the south and sets out second. Then the tent moves, with the Levites in the middle. Ephraim’s group camps on the west and sets out third. Dan’s group camps on the north and sets out last. Israel camps and marches as the LORD commanded.
events.detail: The chapter places three tribes on each side of the tent. The same order holds on the march. Verse 17 puts the tent and the Levites in the middle of the line. Two groups go before it, and two follow. So the tent is never at the edge, in camp or on the road. Every tribe can see where the center is from its own place. Exodus 25:8 gave the reason: God dwells among them.

lds.text: The tent travels in the middle of the tribes (verse 17). What does the camp’s layout put at its center?

events.title: Levites and firstborn
events.summary: Aaron’s sons Eleazar and Ithamar serve as priests after Nadab and Abihu die. The tribe of Levi is given to Aaron to help with the tabernacle. The LORD says he takes the Levites in place of every firstborn in Israel. The firstborn became his on the day he struck Egypt’s firstborn. Levite males a month old and up are counted: 22,000. Their three clans camp around the tent and each has its duties. Israel’s firstborn males number 22,273. The extra 273 are bought back at five shekels each, paid to Aaron.
events.detail: Verse 13 looks back to the night of the exodus. Egypt’s firstborn died, and Israel’s firstborn were spared (Exodus 12:29; 13:2). From then on they belonged to the LORD. Verse 12 makes an exchange: one tribe serves in their place. So every Levite at work reminds Israel of that rescue. The count is exact, and 273 firstborn have no Levite to stand for them. Verses 46–48 require five shekels for each one.

lds.text: The older Church manual connects the firstborn with Israel’s escape from Egypt. The LORD takes the Levites “instead of all the firstborn” (verse 12). When did the firstborn become his (verse 13)?

events.title: Duties for moving the sanctuary
events.summary: The LORD orders a count of Levite men aged thirty to fifty. The sons of Kohath carry the most holy things. First Aaron and his sons cover the ark, table, lamp stand, and altars. The Kohathites must not touch or look at the holy things, or they will die. The sons of Gershon carry the curtains and coverings. The sons of Merari carry the boards, bars, pillars, and sockets. Aaron’s sons Eleazar and Ithamar direct the work. In all, 8,580 Levites are counted for this service.
events.detail: Moving the tent is risky work, and the chapter splits it up. The priests go in first and wrap each holy object (verses 5–14). Only then do the Kohathites come to carry the loads. Verse 15 says they must not touch the holy things “lest they die.” Verses 18–19 show concern for them: “Don’t cut off” these families. The priests’ careful covering is what keeps the carriers alive. Each group depends on another doing its part first.

lds.text: The Kohathites carry what they may not touch or see (verses 15 and 20). Who covers the holy things first?

events.title: Camp, restitution, and jealousy
events.summary: The unclean are sent outside the camp, because the LORD dwells in it. Anyone who wrongs another must confess, repay in full, and add a fifth. If no relative can receive it, the payment goes to the priest. Then comes a law for a husband who suspects his wife and has no witness. He brings her to the priest with a barley offering. The priest mixes holy water with dust from the floor, and she swears an oath. She drinks the water. If guilty, her body swells; if not, she is free and can bear children.
events.detail: Verse 14 names two cases under one feeling. The husband is jealous, and his wife may be guilty or innocent. There is no witness, so no court can settle it (verse 13). The law sets her “before the LORD,” not before her husband (verse 16). Only the husband can start it, and verse 31 clears him either way. Still, he may not punish her on suspicion alone. Verse 28 says an innocent wife “shall be free.”

lds.text: What power does a husband’s accusation give him? What protection does the wife receive? Verse 14 covers a wife who “isn’t defiled.” What does verse 28 say about her?

events.title: Nazirite vows and blessing
events.summary: A man or woman may make a special vow as a Nazirite. For the days of the vow, the person avoids wine and anything from the grapevine. No razor touches the head, and the hair grows long. The person does not go near a dead body, even a parent’s. If someone dies nearby, the vow starts over after cleansing. When the time ends, the Nazirite brings offerings and shaves the head. Then the LORD gives the priests words to bless Israel. They ask the LORD to bless, keep, shine on, and give peace.
events.detail: Priests were born into their office, and only men of Aaron’s family held it. Verse 2 opens a different path: “either man or woman” may take this vow. The rules echo a priest’s. No wine, as for priests on duty (Leviticus 10:9). No contact with the dead, even parents, as for the high priest (Leviticus 21:11). Verse 8 gives the result: the person is “holy to the LORD.” The vow lasts for a stated time and ends with offerings (verse 13).

lds.text: Verse 2 says “either man or woman” may make this vow. What three things does a Nazirite give up in verses 3–6?

events.title: Gifts from the tribal leaders
events.summary: When the tabernacle is set up, the tribal leaders bring six wagons and twelve oxen. Moses gives two wagons to Gershon’s sons and four to Merari’s sons. Kohath’s sons get none, because they carry the holy things on their shoulders. Then each leader brings an offering for the altar, one leader each day. For twelve days every tribe gives the same gift. It is a silver platter, a silver bowl, a gold ladle of incense, and animals. The totals are listed at the end. Moses then hears the LORD’s voice from above the mercy seat.
events.detail: The leaders give six wagons, and Moses does not split them evenly. Gershon’s sons carry curtains and get two (verse 7; 4:25). Merari’s sons carry heavy boards and sockets and get four (verse 8; 4:31–32). Kohath’s sons carry the ark and holy things by hand, so they get none. Each group gets what its load needs. Then verses 12–83 give every tribe the same offering on its own day. So help is shared by need, and honor at the altar is shared equally.

lds.text: The wagons are shared out “according to their service” (verses 7–8). Why do Kohath’s sons get none (verse 9)?

events.title: Levites prepared for service
events.summary: Aaron sets the seven lamps to light the space in front of the lamp stand. The Levites are cleansed with water, shaving, and washed clothes. The whole people gather and lay hands on them. Aaron presents them to the LORD as an offering from Israel. They belong to the LORD in place of Israel’s firstborn. Then they begin their service at the tent under Aaron and his sons. A Levite serves from age twenty-five to fifty. After fifty he stops the heavy work but may still assist his brothers.
events.detail: The Levites’ main work included carrying the tent and its heavy parts (chapter 4). Verses 24–25 set working years from twenty-five to fifty. Verse 26 does not send the older men home. They “assist their brothers” without doing the heavy service. So age changes the task, not the person’s place among the Levites. The people’s hands on the Levites in verse 10 show they serve for all Israel. Verse 19 calls them a gift to Aaron for the people’s sake.

lds.text: A Levite stops the work at fifty but still assists (verses 25–26). What kinds of service fit different stages of life?

events.title: Passover and the guiding cloud
events.summary: In the first month of the second year, Israel keeps the Passover at Sinai. Some men are unclean from touching a dead body and cannot join. They ask Moses why they must be kept back. Moses waits to hear from the LORD. The LORD says anyone unclean or far away may keep it one month later. A foreigner living with Israel may keep it by the same rules. The cloud covers the tabernacle by day and looks like fire by night. Israel camps while it rests and travels when it lifts, however long that takes.
events.detail: The rule was clear: an unclean person could not eat the Passover. These men had touched a dead body (verse 6). In verse 7 they do not ask to break the rule. They ask why they should lose their place in the feast. Moses does not answer from what he already knows. He waits, and the LORD adds a second date one month later (verses 10–11). The new rule also covers travelers, and verse 13 guards it from misuse.

lds.text: Men who were unclean ask why they are kept back (verse 7). What answer does the LORD give in verses 10–11?

events.title: Departure from Sinai
events.summary: The LORD tells Moses to make two silver trumpets. Priests blow them to gather the people, start the march, and mark feasts. On the twentieth day of the second month the cloud lifts. Israel leaves Sinai in order, with Judah’s group first. The Levites carry the tabernacle and the holy things between the groups. Moses asks Hobab the Midianite to come and be their eyes in the wilderness. The ark goes ahead three days to find a resting place. Moses prays when the ark sets out and when it rests.
events.detail: Israel has the cloud, the ark, and the trumpets to lead it. Yet in verse 31 Moses asks a Midianite relative for help. Hobab knows “how we are to encamp in the wilderness.” The cloud shows when and where to stop. A man who knows the wilderness can help with the camping itself. Moses does not treat these as rivals. Verse 32 promises Hobab a share in whatever good the LORD gives Israel.

lds.text: Moses asks Hobab to “be our eyes” (verse 31). Why would Moses want a guide when the cloud leads them?

events.title: Complaints, elders, and quail
events.summary: The people complain, and the LORD’s fire burns the edge of the camp. Then they weep for meat and remember the fish and vegetables of Egypt. They say they are tired of manna. Moses tells the LORD the burden is too heavy and asks to die. The LORD has him gather seventy elders and puts the Spirit on them. Eldad and Medad prophesy in the camp, and Moses wishes all the people were prophets. A wind brings quail, piled around the camp. While the people are still eating, a plague strikes them.
events.detail: Verse 5 gives the people’s memory of Egypt: fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, garlic. They say they ate it “for nothing.” Exodus 1:13–14 said their lives there were bitter with hard service. They ate that food as slaves. Their craving has changed what they remember. Verse 6 shows the effect: manna becomes “nothing at all.” Verse 20 names the root: they have rejected the LORD who is among them.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies gratitude and meekness here. Joshua wants Eldad and Medad stopped (verse 28). What does Moses wish for in verse 29?

events.title: Miriam and Aaron challenge Moses
events.summary: Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses because of his Cushite wife. They ask if the LORD has spoken only through Moses. The text says Moses was very humble. The LORD calls all three to the tent and comes down in the cloud. He says he speaks to Moses plainly, mouth to mouth, not in dreams. When the cloud leaves, Miriam’s skin is leprous and white as snow. Aaron begs Moses, and Moses cries, “Heal her, God.” She is shut outside the camp seven days, and the people wait for her.
events.detail: Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses, and the LORD defends him (verses 6–8). Moses himself says nothing until verse 13. His only words in the chapter are a prayer for her healing. The LORD sets a limit of seven days outside the camp. Verse 15 adds what the people did: they did not travel until she returned. The whole camp, with the cloud and the ark, waits for one person. Her correction is real, and so is her place among them.

lds.text: The Church lesson studies respect for prophetic service. Moses prays for the sister who spoke against him (verse 13). What do the people do while she is outside the camp (verse 15)?

events.title: The spies report on Canaan
events.summary: The LORD tells Moses to send one leader from each tribe into Canaan. Moses tells them to look at the land, the people, and the cities. They travel forty days and bring back a huge cluster of grapes. They report that the land flows with milk and honey. They also say the people are strong and the cities walled. Caleb says Israel should go up at once and is well able to win. The others say the people are too strong. They spread a bad report and say they felt like grasshoppers.
events.detail: Moses asked for facts in verses 18–20: the land, the people, the cities. Verses 27–29 answer with facts, and no one disputes them. The split comes with the conclusion. Caleb says, “We are well able” (verse 30). The others say, “We aren’t able” (verse 31). Then verse 32 calls their next words “an evil report.” They now say the land eats its people and that they looked like grasshoppers.

lds.text: The Church lesson studies Caleb’s faith. Caleb and the others saw the same land (verses 27–31). Where do their reports differ?

events.title: The people refuse to enter
events.summary: The people weep all night and want to choose a leader and return to Egypt. Joshua and Caleb say the land is good and the LORD is with them. The people talk of stoning them. The LORD threatens to destroy them, and Moses pleads God’s name and mercy. The LORD pardons, but that generation will die in the wilderness over forty years. Only Caleb and Joshua will enter, with the children. The ten spies die of plague. The people then go up without Moses or the ark and are beaten back.
events.detail: In verse 40 the people say, “We have sinned,” and set out to fight. It looks like the obedience they refused the day before. Moses tells them the LORD is not with them now (verses 42–43). Verse 44 says they “presumed to go up” anyway. The ark and Moses stayed in the camp. So this is a second act of not listening, not a repair of the first. Verse 45 reports the defeat that Moses had warned of.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects this account with hope through faith. The people go up after being told not to (verses 41–44). What stayed in the camp?

events.title: Offerings and reminders
events.summary: The LORD gives rules for offerings once Israel lives in the land. Each animal offering comes with set amounts of flour, oil, and wine. The same rule applies to the foreigner living among them. The first of each batch of dough is given to the LORD. Sins done by mistake are forgiven through an offering. A person who sins with a high hand is cut off. A man found gathering sticks on the Sabbath is stoned at the LORD’s word. Israel must wear fringes with a blue cord to remember the commandments.
events.detail: Chapter 14 showed a people led by what their eyes saw in Canaan (13:33). Verse 39 warns against following “your own heart and your own eyes.” The answer is something else to look at. A fringe with a blue cord hangs on every garment (verse 38). The order of verbs is see, remember, do. The reminder is worn all day, in ordinary work and travel. Verse 41 ties it to the exodus: the God who brought them out.

lds.text: How can a visible reminder help someone remember a promise? The fringe is there “that you may see it” (verse 39). What does seeing it guard against?

events.title: Korah, Dathan, and Abiram rebel
events.summary: Korah the Levite, with Dathan, Abiram, and 250 leaders, rises against Moses and Aaron. They say all the people are holy and ask why Moses lifts himself above them. Moses tells Korah’s group to bring pans of incense before the LORD. Dathan and Abiram refuse to come and accuse Moses of failing them. The ground opens and swallows the rebels’ households. Fire burns up the 250 men with their incense pans. The next day the people blame Moses and Aaron, and a plague starts. Aaron runs in with incense and stands between the dead and the living.
events.detail: Korah’s claim in verse 3 starts from something true. God did call all Israel a holy nation (Exodus 19:6). Korah uses it to say no one should hold a special duty. Moses hears a different aim in verse 10: Korah wants the priesthood too. The chapter then shows what the priest’s place is for. In verses 46–48 Aaron runs into the plague with incense and makes atonement. He stands “between the dead and the living,” at risk to himself.

lds.text: The manual studies priestly authority. Korah says “all the congregation are holy” (verse 3). What does Aaron do for the people in verses 47–48?

events.title: Aaron’s staff buds
events.summary: The LORD tells Moses to collect a rod from the leader of each tribe. Each man’s name is written on his rod, and Aaron’s name is on Levi’s. Moses lays the twelve rods in the tent before the covenant. The rod of the man God chooses will bud. The next day Aaron’s rod has buds, blossoms, and ripe almonds. Each leader takes his own rod back. Aaron’s rod is kept in the tent as a sign against rebels. The people cry that anyone who comes near the tabernacle will die.
events.detail: Chapter 16 ended the revolt with deaths, and the people still complained (16:41). Chapter 17 answers the same question without killing anyone. Twelve dead sticks spend a night in the tent. Only Aaron’s shows life: buds, flowers, and almonds at once (verse 8). Verse 10 says why it is kept: to end the complaints “that they not die.” So the sign is meant to protect the people. Their fear in verses 12–13 leads into the duties of chapter 18.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: How does Aaron’s flowering staff answer the dispute about leadership? Why is the rod kept (verse 10)?

events.title: Priestly duties and support
events.summary: The LORD tells Aaron that the priests answer for the sanctuary. The Levites help them but may not touch the holy vessels or the altar. The priests receive the holy offerings, first fruits, and firstborn animals as their food. Firstborn sons and unclean animals are bought back for five shekels. Aaron gets no land, because the LORD is his portion. The Levites receive Israel’s tithe, a tenth, in return for their service. They also get no land. From the tithe they must give a tenth, the best part, to the priest.
events.detail: The people ended chapter 17 afraid to go near the tent (17:13). Chapter 18 answers by naming who bears that risk. The priests and Levites do the service “that there be no more wrath” (verse 5). Verse 21 gives the Levites the tithe, since they get no land (verse 24). The gift is called pay for service, not a favor. It also brings a duty: a tenth of it goes to the priests (verse 26). Those supported by gifts are themselves givers.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: The Levites receive the tithe for their work (verse 21). What must they give from it in verse 26?

events.title: The red heifer and cleansing
events.summary: Israel brings a red heifer, a young cow never yoked and without defect. It is killed and burned outside the camp with cedar, hyssop, and scarlet. Its ashes are stored and mixed with running water for cleansing. Anyone who touches a dead body is unclean for seven days. So is anyone in a tent of death, or who touches a bone or grave. A clean person sprinkles the water on them on the third and seventh days. Then they wash and are clean at evening. Whoever refuses the cleansing defiles the sanctuary and is cut off.
events.detail: Everyone will have to touch the dead at some time, to bury family. Verse 11 does not call this a sin. It sets a seven-day state with a fixed way out. The cleansing water is made ahead and kept ready for anyone (verse 9). A mourner cannot do the sprinkling alone. Verses 18–19 require “a clean person” to do it, on two set days. The one case that is punished is refusing the cleansing (verses 13 and 20).
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: What care do people need after a death? Touching the dead makes a person unclean seven days (verse 11). What does someone else do for that person in verses 18–19?

events.title: Miriam dies, water flows, and Aaron dies
events.summary: Miriam dies at Kadesh. There is no water, and the people quarrel with Moses and Aaron. The LORD tells Moses to take the rod and speak to the rock. Moses calls the people rebels and strikes the rock twice, and water pours out. The LORD says they did not believe him and will not bring Israel in. Edom refuses to let Israel pass through, even for payment. At Mount Hor, Moses puts Aaron’s garments on his son Eleazar. Aaron dies there, and Israel weeps thirty days.
events.detail: Verse 8 told Moses to speak to the rock before the people. In verse 10 Moses speaks to the people and calls them rebels. He says “we” will bring the water, and he strikes the rock twice. The water still comes, and the people drink. Verse 12 gives God’s charge: they did not believe him or show him holy. Long service does not exempt Moses. The chapter begins with Miriam’s death and ends with Aaron’s.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Moses’s choices under pressure. Moses was told to speak to the rock (verse 8). What did he say and do in verses 10–11?

events.title: The bronze serpent and eastern victories
events.summary: The king of Arad attacks, and Israel defeats him after a vow to the LORD. On the road around Edom the people speak against God and Moses. They call the manna disgusting food. The LORD sends venomous snakes, and many die. The people confess, and Moses prays. Moses sets a bronze snake on a pole, and whoever looks at it lives. Israel travels on and sings at a well. They defeat the kings Sihon and Og and take their land.
events.detail: The people ask Moses to pray that the snakes be taken away (verse 7). The LORD does not remove them. He gives a cure that each bitten person must use. Verse 9 states it simply: one who “looked at the serpent of bronze” lived. The cure has the shape of the thing that harmed them. Second Kings 18:4 reports that Israel later burned incense to this bronze snake. King Hezekiah broke it in pieces.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects the serpent with looking to Christ. Compare Alma 33 and Helaman 8. What did a bitten person have to do to live (verse 9)?

events.title: Balak sends for Balaam
events.summary: Israel camps in the plains of Moab, and Moab is afraid. King Balak sends for Balaam to curse Israel. God tells Balaam not to go, because the people are blessed. Balak sends higher princes and promises great honor. God lets Balaam go but only to say what God tells him. The donkey sees the LORD’s angel with a sword and turns aside three times. Balaam beats her, and the LORD opens her mouth to speak. Then Balaam sees the angel, who lets him go on with the same warning.
events.detail: Balaam is hired as a man who sees and speaks for the gods (verse 6). On this road his donkey sees the angel three times, and he sees nothing. He beats her each time. The LORD opens her mouth (verse 28) and then Balaam’s eyes (verse 31). The famous seer needed both done for him. The angel says the donkey saved his life (verse 33). It prepares for chapter 23, where Balaam can say only what he is given.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies how Balaam responds to pressure from the king. Who sees the angel first in verses 23–27?

events.title: Balaam blesses Israel
events.summary: Balaam has Balak build seven altars and offer bulls and rams. The LORD puts a word in Balaam’s mouth. Balaam asks how he can curse those whom God has not cursed. Balak takes him to a second place, where he sees only part of Israel. Seven more altars are built. Balaam says God is not a man who lies or changes his mind. God has blessed, and Balaam cannot reverse it. Balak takes him to a third place, the top of Peor.
events.detail: Balak’s plan in verse 13 is to change the view. From the new spot Balaam will see “just part of them.” A smaller Israel might seem easier to curse. He also repeats the full offering: seven altars, seven bulls, seven rams (verse 14). Verse 19 answers both moves. God is not a man who lies or changes his mind. Balak can move the seer, but he cannot move the one who speaks through him.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Balak moves Balaam to a new place to get a new answer (verse 13). What does Balaam say about God in verse 19?

events.title: A star and a scepter
events.summary: Balaam sees that the LORD wants to bless Israel and uses no omens this time. The Spirit of God comes on him as he looks at Israel’s tents. He says their tents are lovely, like gardens by a river. He says those who bless Israel are blessed, and those who curse it are cursed. Balak is furious and sends him home without the promised honor. Balaam reminds him that no amount of silver could change the LORD’s word. He says a star will come from Jacob and a scepter from Israel. He speaks against Moab, Edom, Amalek, and others, and goes home.
events.detail: Balak hired Balaam with the promise of “great honor” (22:17). After three blessings he cancels the reward in verse 11. He even blames the LORD for the lost pay. Balaam repeats his first answer (verse 13; 22:18). A house full of silver could not change the LORD’s word. Then Balaam gives a fourth saying that no one paid for (verses 15–19). Numbers 31:16 later reports that Balaam did harm Israel by other advice.

lds.text: The Church manual connects the star and scepter with Christ. Balak says the LORD kept Balaam from honor (verse 11). How does Balaam answer in verse 13?

events.title: Peor and Phinehas
events.summary: At Shittim, Israelite men go after Moabite women and join the sacrifices to their gods. Israel joins itself to Baal of Peor, and the LORD’s anger burns. Moses orders the judges to put the guilty to death. An Israelite man brings a Midianite woman into the camp while the people weep. Phinehas, Aaron’s grandson, kills them both with a spear. A plague stops after twenty-four thousand have died. The LORD gives Phinehas a covenant of peace and a lasting priesthood. The LORD tells Moses to treat the Midianites as enemies.
events.detail: The crisis here is worship of another god, not marriage (verses 2–3). Zimri brings Cozbi past the weeping people in open view (verse 6). Phinehas kills them, and verse 8 says the plague stopped. Verses 11–13 praise him and call the act atonement. The reward is named “peace,” which sits oddly beside a spear. The text presents the killing as ending a greater loss of life. It does not hide the violence.

lds.text: Phinehas is given “my covenant of peace” after a killing (verses 12–13). What had stopped in verse 8?

events.title: The second census
events.summary: After the plague the LORD orders a new count of men twenty and older. Moses and Eleazar count them in the plains of Moab by the Jordan. The list recalls Dathan, Abiram, and Korah, and notes that Korah’s sons did not die. It names Zelophehad’s five daughters. The total is 601,730. The land will be divided by these names: larger groups get more, smaller groups less. The place of each share is chosen by lot. No one from the first count is left except Caleb and Joshua.
events.detail: The first count in chapter 1 was for war. This count has a second use, stated in verse 53: dividing the land. Verse 54 sets the size of each share by the number of names. Verse 55 leaves the location to the lot. So no tribe can claim the best ground by strength. The total is nearly the same as in the first count (1:46). Verses 64–65 note that it is a new generation, as 14:29 foretold.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Verse 64 says no one from the first count remained. Who are the two men named in verse 65?

events.title: The daughters’ petition and Joshua’s appointment
events.summary: Zelophehad’s five daughters come before Moses, the priest, and the leaders. Their father died in the wilderness and left no son. They ask for land among their father’s brothers so his name is not lost. Moses brings their case to the LORD. The LORD says the daughters are right and must receive the inheritance. He makes it a rule: with no son, the land goes to a daughter. Then the LORD tells Moses he will see the land and die. Moses asks for a new leader and lays hands on Joshua before the people.
events.detail: Land was to be divided by the names of men counted in chapter 26. A man with no sons would drop out of the list. Five sisters, each named in verse 1, speak at the tent door before everyone. Verse 4 asks why their father’s name should be taken away. Moses has no ruling ready and takes the case to the LORD (verse 5). The answer is “The daughters of Zelophehad speak right.” Their case then becomes law for all Israel (verses 8–11).

lds.text: Consider how careful listening can reveal a gap in existing rules. The manual also studies Joshua’s appointment. What do the five daughters ask for in verse 4?

events.title: Daily, Sabbath, and festival offerings
events.summary: The LORD tells Israel to bring his offerings at their set times. Two lambs are offered every day, one in the morning and one at evening. Each comes with flour, oil, and a drink offering. Two more lambs are offered every Sabbath. At each new month there are bulls, a ram, and seven lambs. Passover is on the fourteenth day of the first month. Seven days of unleavened bread follow, with offerings each day. The feast of weeks has its own offerings.
events.detail: Verse 2 calls these offerings “my food,” due “in their due season.” The chapter then moves from the smallest unit of time to larger ones. Every day has two lambs (verses 3–4). Every Sabbath adds two more (verse 9). Every month and each feast add still more (verses 11 and 19). The offerings come from the whole people, not from one giver. So the calendar keeps a steady claim on Israel’s flocks and fields.
