lds.text: The daily offering is two lambs, morning and evening (verses 3–4). How can repeated acts sustain remembrance and gratitude?

events.title: Offerings in the seventh month
events.summary: The seventh month has three sacred times. The first day is a day of trumpets with rest and offerings. The tenth day is a day to humble oneself and do no work. On the fifteenth day a seven-day feast begins. Thirteen bulls are offered the first day, and one fewer each day after. On the seventh day there are seven bulls. The eighth day is a solemn assembly with one bull. These offerings are in addition to vows and free gifts.
events.detail: The feast week has the most offerings in these two chapters. Verses 12–34 count down: thirteen bulls, then twelve, down to seven. Each day’s rams and lambs stay the same. Verse 35 marks an eighth day with a “solemn assembly” and no regular work. Its offering is small: one bull, one ram, seven lambs. So the busiest week of offerings ends in a quiet day. Verse 39 adds that all of this is apart from personal vows and gifts.

lds.text: The feast offerings drop from thirteen bulls to seven, then one (verses 13, 32, 36). How can a calendar help a community remember its duties together?

events.title: Vows and household authority
events.summary: Moses tells the tribal heads the LORD’s rule on vows. A man who vows must not break his word. A young woman’s vow stands if her father hears it and says nothing. If he forbids it that day, it does not stand, and the LORD forgives her. A wife’s vow stands if her husband hears and says nothing. If he forbids it that day, it is void. A widow’s or divorced woman’s vow stands. A husband who cancels a vow later bears her guilt.
events.detail: Verse 2 sets the base rule: a vow must be kept. The rest deals with women under a father or husband. He may cancel her vow only on the day he hears it (verses 5, 8). Verse 14 says silence counts as consent: he “establishes” it by saying nothing. After that he cannot undo it without bearing her guilt (verse 15). So the law limits his power by a deadline. Verse 9 shows a widow or divorced woman answers for her own vows.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Who can cancel a vow in these laws? How does that power affect family members? What does a husband’s silence do in verse 14?

events.title: War against Midian
events.summary: The LORD tells Moses to take vengeance on Midian before he dies. Twelve thousand men go to war with Phinehas the priest. They kill Midian’s men, its five kings, and Balaam. They bring back the women, children, and herds. Moses is angry that the women were spared, because of what happened at Peor. He orders the boys and the women who have lain with a man killed. The soldiers purify themselves seven days outside the camp. The plunder is divided, and the officers give gold because no soldier was lost.
events.detail: The chapter presents this war as the LORD’s answer to Peor (verses 2 and 16). The army returns as winners, and Moses meets them with anger. Verse 17 orders the killing of boys and of women who have known a man. Verse 18 keeps the young girls alive for the soldiers. The text reports these orders without softening them. It then requires every fighter to stay outside the camp and be purified (verse 19). Even a commanded war leaves those who killed unclean.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: How does war affect the families in this chapter? Whom does verse 17 name?

events.title: Eastern tribes make a promise
events.summary: Reuben and Gad have large herds and want the grazing land east of the Jordan. They ask Moses for it and ask not to cross the river. Moses asks if their brothers should go to war while they sit there. He says they are acting like the spies who discouraged Israel. They promise to build towns for their families and then fight in front of Israel. They will not go home until every tribe has its land. Moses agrees and warns that their sin will find them out if they fail. He gives them and half of Manasseh the lands of Sihon and Og.
events.detail: Reuben and Gad ask for land already won, east of the river. Their last words in verse 5 are “Don’t bring us over the Jordan.” Moses hears a threat to everyone else. If two tribes stay home, the rest may lose heart, as at Kadesh. The answer is a bargain made in public. They get the land if their fighters cross and stay to the end. Their gain is allowed, but it comes with a duty to the other tribes.

lds.text: Moses asks if their brothers should fight while they sit (verse 6). What do Reuben and Gad promise in verses 17–18?

events.title: The journey remembered
events.summary: Moses writes down the stages of Israel’s journey at the LORD’s command. The list begins at Rameses, the day after the Passover. Egypt is burying its firstborn as Israel leaves. Dozens of camps are named, from the Red Sea to Sinai to Kadesh. Aaron dies on Mount Hor in the fortieth year, at age 123. The list ends in the plains of Moab by the Jordan. The LORD tells Israel to drive out Canaan’s people and destroy their idols. Any who remain will be like thorns in Israel’s sides.
events.detail: Verse 2 says Moses wrote these stages “by the commandment of the LORD.” So the record itself is commanded, not only the travel. Most of the entries are just two verbs: they traveled, they camped. A few stop for a memory: the Passover night, Elim’s water, Aaron’s death. The list includes the hard places with the good ones. Forty years of wandering become a line a reader can follow. It ends at the Jordan, with orders for the next step (verses 50–53).

lds.text: Why might a community keep a list of the places along its journey? Who wrote this list, and at whose command (verse 2)?

events.title: Borders and appointed leaders
events.summary: The LORD gives Moses the borders of the land of Canaan. The south border runs from the Salt Sea along Edom. The Great Sea is the west border. The north and east borders are traced, ending at the Jordan and the Salt Sea. This land is for the nine and a half tribes, by lot. Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh already have land east of the Jordan. Eleazar the priest and Joshua will divide the land. One leader from each tribe is named to help, with Caleb for Judah.
events.detail: The first half of the chapter draws a border before any land is taken. The second half names the people who will divide it. Eleazar the priest and Joshua lead (verse 17). Verse 18 adds one leader from every tribe that will receive land. So each tribe has its own person present when shares are set. Caleb, who trusted the promise in 13:30, stands for Judah. Naming the dividers ahead of time leaves less room for dispute later.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: What helps people share land fairly? Verses 17–18 name who will divide it. Who are they?

events.title: Levite towns and cities of refuge
events.summary: Israel must give the Levites forty-eight towns with pasture land around them. Six of these are cities of refuge. A person who kills someone by accident may flee there from the avenger. He must not die before he stands trial before the community. One who killed with a weapon or from hatred is put to death. One who killed without hatred stays in the city until the high priest dies. No one is put to death on one witness alone. No payment can free a murderer, because blood pollutes the land.
events.detail: A dead person’s relative, the “avenger of blood,” could kill the killer (verse 19). The city of refuge puts a wall between them for a time. Verse 12 gives the purpose: no death before a trial by the community. The trial asks about intent: a weapon, hatred, or lying in wait (verses 16–23). Verse 30 requires more than one witness for a death sentence. Verse 31 forbids a rich killer from paying his way out. So revenge is held back until the facts are judged.
events.uncertainty: Markers show regions or traditional identifications. Many campsites, the sea crossing, and Mount Hor lack secure locations.

lds.text: Consider how fair judgment requires more than an accusation. The city protects the killer “until he stands before the congregation” (verse 12). How many witnesses does verse 30 require?

events.title: Inheritance and marriage
events.summary: The family heads of Manasseh come to Moses with a problem. Zelophehad’s daughters will inherit land. If they marry men of another tribe, the land will pass to that tribe. Moses answers by the LORD’s word that they speak rightly. The daughters may marry whom they think best, but only within their father’s tribe. Any daughter who inherits land must do the same. The five daughters marry sons of their father’s brothers. So their land stays in Manasseh, and the book ends in the plains of Moab.
events.detail: Chapter 27 gave the daughters their father’s land. This chapter deals with a side effect. Land followed the husband’s tribe, so their marriages could move it (verse 3). Verse 6 keeps two things together. The women choose: “whom they think best.” The choice is limited: within their father’s tribe. Their right to the land is kept, at the cost of a narrower choice.

lds.text: How do the inheritance rules affect Zelophehad’s daughters and their choices? What two things does verse 6 say about whom they may marry?

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway. The line follows Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time. Exodus 13:17 names a near road, “the way of the land of the Philistines.” The encyclopedia article lists that name for this coast road.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route mostly from Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria. The line follows Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route mostly from Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.

ancientRoads.title: Central ridge road
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south road followed the central hills. It passed Beersheba, Hebron, Jerusalem, Bethel, and Shechem. It continued toward the Jezreel Valley.
ancientRoads.detail: This route linked the principal highland settlements of Judah and Israel. It avoided some lowland obstacles but still depended on ridges, saddles, and local descents. The line follows Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route mostly from Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.

ancientRoads.title: Jordan Valley and Arabah route
ancientRoads.summary: A long north–south route used the Arabah and Jordan Valley. It joined Aqaba, the Dead Sea, Jericho, Beth Shean, and Galilee.
ancientRoads.detail: Travelers used several tracks on both sides of the valley. Fords and seasonal conditions affected where people crossed the Jordan. The line follows Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route mostly from Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.

ancientRoads.title: Shephelah road
ancientRoads.summary: This route ran through Judah’s western lowlands. It joined Beersheba, Lachish, Gezer, Aphek, and the valleys below Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.detail: The Shephelah formed a connected lowland zone between the coastal plain and the Judean hills. Fortified towns near the route guarded approaches into the highlands. The line follows Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route mostly from Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem. The line follows Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.

ancientRoads.title: Jerusalem–Jericho road
ancientRoads.summary: This steep east–west route connected Jerusalem with Jericho and the Jordan Valley. It also reached crossings toward Transjordan.
ancientRoads.detail: The road descended rapidly through dry and broken terrain. It gave Jerusalem access to the valley and to routes east of the Jordan. The line follows Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.

ancientRoads.title: Transjordan plateau route

ancientRoads.detail: This series of plateau roads is often called the King’s Highway. It supported trade east of the Jordan. It linked nearby towns with Arabia, Syria, and western crossings. The line follows Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time. Numbers 20:17 and 21:22 name “the king’s highway” east of the Jordan.

guides.title: Numbers: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Memory changes under pressure
steps.text: Verse 5 gives the people’s memory of Egypt: fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, garlic. They say they ate it “for nothing.” Exodus 1:13–14 said their lives there were bitter with hard service. They ate that food as slaves. Their craving has changed what they remember. Verse 6 shows the effect: manna becomes “nothing at all.” Verse 20 names the root: they have rejected the LORD who is among them.

steps.title: An outsider sees what a seer misses
steps.text: Balaam is hired as a man who sees and speaks for the gods (verse 6). On this road his donkey sees the angel three times, and he sees nothing. He beats her each time. The LORD opens her mouth (verse 28) and then Balaam’s eyes (verse 31). The famous seer needed both done for him. The angel says the donkey saved his life (verse 33). It prepares for chapter 23, where Balaam can say only what he is given.

steps.title: A family’s case changes the rule
steps.text: Land was to be divided by the names of men counted in chapter 26. A man with no sons would drop out of the list. Five sisters, each named in verse 1, speak at the tent door before everyone. Verse 4 asks why their father’s name should be taken away. Moses has no ruling ready and takes the case to the LORD (verse 5). The answer is “The daughters of Zelophehad speak right.” Their case then becomes law for all Israel (verses 8–11).

chapterMaps.narrative: In the second year after Egypt, the LORD tells Moses to count Israel. The count covers men twenty and older who can go to war. One leader from each tribe helps Moses and Aaron. Each tribe is counted by families and fathers’ houses. The total is 603,550. The Levites are not counted with the rest. They care for the tabernacle, carry it, and camp around it. No outsider may come near it.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD arranges the camp around the Tent of Meeting. Each tribe camps under its own banner, at a distance from the tent. Judah’s group camps on the east and sets out first. Reuben’s group camps on the south and sets out second. Then the tent moves, with the Levites in the middle. Ephraim’s group camps on the west and sets out third. Dan’s group camps on the north and sets out last. Israel camps and marches as the LORD commanded.

chapterMaps.narrative: Aaron’s sons Eleazar and Ithamar serve as priests after Nadab and Abihu die. The tribe of Levi is given to Aaron to help with the tabernacle. The LORD says he takes the Levites in place of every firstborn in Israel. The firstborn became his on the day he struck Egypt’s firstborn. Levite males a month old and up are counted: 22,000. Their three clans camp around the tent and each has its duties. Israel’s firstborn males number 22,273. The extra 273 are bought back at five shekels each, paid to Aaron.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD orders a count of Levite men aged thirty to fifty. The sons of Kohath carry the most holy things. First Aaron and his sons cover the ark, table, lamp stand, and altars. The Kohathites must not touch or look at the holy things, or they will die. The sons of Gershon carry the curtains and coverings. The sons of Merari carry the boards, bars, pillars, and sockets. Aaron’s sons Eleazar and Ithamar direct the work. In all, 8,580 Levites are counted for this service.

chapterMaps.narrative: The unclean are sent outside the camp, because the LORD dwells in it. Anyone who wrongs another must confess, repay in full, and add a fifth. If no relative can receive it, the payment goes to the priest. Then comes a law for a husband who suspects his wife and has no witness. He brings her to the priest with a barley offering. The priest mixes holy water with dust from the floor, and she swears an oath. She drinks the water. If guilty, her body swells; if not, she is free and can bear children.

chapterMaps.narrative: A man or woman may make a special vow as a Nazirite. For the days of the vow, the person avoids wine and anything from the grapevine. No razor touches the head, and the hair grows long. The person does not go near a dead body, even a parent’s. If someone dies nearby, the vow starts over after cleansing. When the time ends, the Nazirite brings offerings and shaves the head. Then the LORD gives the priests words to bless Israel. They ask the LORD to bless, keep, shine on, and give peace.

chapterMaps.narrative: When the tabernacle is set up, the tribal leaders bring six wagons and twelve oxen. Moses gives two wagons to Gershon’s sons and four to Merari’s sons. Kohath’s sons get none, because they carry the holy things on their shoulders. Then each leader brings an offering for the altar, one leader each day. For twelve days every tribe gives the same gift. It is a silver platter, a silver bowl, a gold ladle of incense, and animals. The totals are listed at the end. Moses then hears the LORD’s voice from above the mercy seat.

chapterMaps.narrative: Aaron sets the seven lamps to light the space in front of the lamp stand. The Levites are cleansed with water, shaving, and washed clothes. The whole people gather and lay hands on them. Aaron presents them to the LORD as an offering from Israel. They belong to the LORD in place of Israel’s firstborn. Then they begin their service at the tent under Aaron and his sons. A Levite serves from age twenty-five to fifty. After fifty he stops the heavy work but may still assist his brothers.

chapterMaps.narrative: In the first month of the second year, Israel keeps the Passover at Sinai. Some men are unclean from touching a dead body and cannot join. They ask Moses why they must be kept back. Moses waits to hear from the LORD. The LORD says anyone unclean or far away may keep it one month later. A foreigner living with Israel may keep it by the same rules. The cloud covers the tabernacle by day and looks like fire by night. Israel camps while it rests and travels when it lifts, however long that takes.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD tells Moses to make two silver trumpets. Priests blow them to gather the people, start the march, and mark feasts. On the twentieth day of the second month the cloud lifts. Israel leaves Sinai in order, with Judah’s group first. The Levites carry the tabernacle and the holy things between the groups. Moses asks Hobab the Midianite to come and be their eyes in the wilderness. The ark goes ahead three days to find a resting place. Moses prays when the ark sets out and when it rests.

chapterMaps.narrative: The people complain, and the LORD’s fire burns the edge of the camp. Then they weep for meat and remember the fish and vegetables of Egypt. They say they are tired of manna. Moses tells the LORD the burden is too heavy and asks to die. The LORD has him gather seventy elders and puts the Spirit on them. Eldad and Medad prophesy in the camp, and Moses wishes all the people were prophets. A wind brings quail, piled around the camp. While the people are still eating, a plague strikes them.

chapterMaps.narrative: Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses because of his Cushite wife. They ask if the LORD has spoken only through Moses. The text says Moses was very humble. The LORD calls all three to the tent and comes down in the cloud. He says he speaks to Moses plainly, mouth to mouth, not in dreams. When the cloud leaves, Miriam’s skin is leprous and white as snow. Aaron begs Moses, and Moses cries, “Heal her, God.” She is shut outside the camp seven days, and the people wait for her.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD tells Moses to send one leader from each tribe into Canaan. Moses tells them to look at the land, the people, and the cities. They travel forty days and bring back a huge cluster of grapes. They report that the land flows with milk and honey. They also say the people are strong and the cities walled. Caleb says Israel should go up at once and is well able to win. The others say the people are too strong. They spread a bad report and say they felt like grasshoppers.

chapterMaps.narrative: The people weep all night and want to choose a leader and return to Egypt. Joshua and Caleb say the land is good and the LORD is with them. The people talk of stoning them. The LORD threatens to destroy them, and Moses pleads God’s name and mercy. The LORD pardons, but that generation will die in the wilderness over forty years. Only Caleb and Joshua will enter, with the children. The ten spies die of plague. The people then go up without Moses or the ark and are beaten back.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD gives rules for offerings once Israel lives in the land. Each animal offering comes with set amounts of flour, oil, and wine. The same rule applies to the foreigner living among them. The first of each batch of dough is given to the LORD. Sins done by mistake are forgiven through an offering. A person who sins with a high hand is cut off. A man found gathering sticks on the Sabbath is stoned at the LORD’s word. Israel must wear fringes with a blue cord to remember the commandments.

chapterMaps.narrative: Korah the Levite, with Dathan, Abiram, and 250 leaders, rises against Moses and Aaron. They say all the people are holy and ask why Moses lifts himself above them. Moses tells Korah’s group to bring pans of incense before the LORD. Dathan and Abiram refuse to come and accuse Moses of failing them. The ground opens and swallows the rebels’ households. Fire burns up the 250 men with their incense pans. The next day the people blame Moses and Aaron, and a plague starts. Aaron runs in with incense and stands between the dead and the living.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD tells Moses to collect a rod from the leader of each tribe. Each man’s name is written on his rod, and Aaron’s name is on Levi’s. Moses lays the twelve rods in the tent before the covenant. The rod of the man God chooses will bud. The next day Aaron’s rod has buds, blossoms, and ripe almonds. Each leader takes his own rod back. Aaron’s rod is kept in the tent as a sign against rebels. The people cry that anyone who comes near the tabernacle will die.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD tells Aaron that the priests answer for the sanctuary. The Levites help them but may not touch the holy vessels or the altar. The priests receive the holy offerings, first fruits, and firstborn animals as their food. Firstborn sons and unclean animals are bought back for five shekels. Aaron gets no land, because the LORD is his portion. The Levites receive Israel’s tithe, a tenth, in return for their service. They also get no land. From the tithe they must give a tenth, the best part, to the priest.

chapterMaps.narrative: Israel brings a red heifer, a young cow never yoked and without defect. It is killed and burned outside the camp with cedar, hyssop, and scarlet. Its ashes are stored and mixed with running water for cleansing. Anyone who touches a dead body is unclean for seven days. So is anyone in a tent of death, or who touches a bone or grave. A clean person sprinkles the water on them on the third and seventh days. Then they wash and are clean at evening. Whoever refuses the cleansing defiles the sanctuary and is cut off.

chapterMaps.narrative: Miriam dies at Kadesh. There is no water, and the people quarrel with Moses and Aaron. The LORD tells Moses to take the rod and speak to the rock. Moses calls the people rebels and strikes the rock twice, and water pours out. The LORD says they did not believe him and will not bring Israel in. Edom refuses to let Israel pass through, even for payment. At Mount Hor, Moses puts Aaron’s garments on his son Eleazar. Aaron dies there, and Israel weeps thirty days.

chapterMaps.narrative: The king of Arad attacks, and Israel defeats him after a vow to the LORD. On the road around Edom the people speak against God and Moses. They call the manna disgusting food. The LORD sends venomous snakes, and many die. The people confess, and Moses prays. Moses sets a bronze snake on a pole, and whoever looks at it lives. Israel travels on and sings at a well. They defeat the kings Sihon and Og and take their land.

chapterMaps.narrative: Israel camps in the plains of Moab, and Moab is afraid. King Balak sends for Balaam to curse Israel. God tells Balaam not to go, because the people are blessed. Balak sends higher princes and promises great honor. God lets Balaam go but only to say what God tells him. The donkey sees the LORD’s angel with a sword and turns aside three times. Balaam beats her, and the LORD opens her mouth to speak. Then Balaam sees the angel, who lets him go on with the same warning.

chapterMaps.narrative: Balaam has Balak build seven altars and offer bulls and rams. The LORD puts a word in Balaam’s mouth. Balaam asks how he can curse those whom God has not cursed. Balak takes him to a second place, where he sees only part of Israel. Seven more altars are built. Balaam says God is not a man who lies or changes his mind. God has blessed, and Balaam cannot reverse it. Balak takes him to a third place, the top of Peor.

chapterMaps.narrative: Balaam sees that the LORD wants to bless Israel and uses no omens this time. The Spirit of God comes on him as he looks at Israel’s tents. He says their tents are lovely, like gardens by a river. He says those who bless Israel are blessed, and those who curse it are cursed. Balak is furious and sends him home without the promised honor. Balaam reminds him that no amount of silver could change the LORD’s word. He says a star will come from Jacob and a scepter from Israel. He speaks against Moab, Edom, Amalek, and others, and goes home.

chapterMaps.narrative: At Shittim, Israelite men go after Moabite women and join the sacrifices to their gods. Israel joins itself to Baal of Peor, and the LORD’s anger burns. Moses orders the judges to put the guilty to death. An Israelite man brings a Midianite woman into the camp while the people weep. Phinehas, Aaron’s grandson, kills them both with a spear. A plague stops after twenty-four thousand have died. The LORD gives Phinehas a covenant of peace and a lasting priesthood. The LORD tells Moses to treat the Midianites as enemies.

chapterMaps.narrative: After the plague the LORD orders a new count of men twenty and older. Moses and Eleazar count them in the plains of Moab by the Jordan. The list recalls Dathan, Abiram, and Korah, and notes that Korah’s sons did not die. It names Zelophehad’s five daughters. The total is 601,730. The land will be divided by these names: larger groups get more, smaller groups less. The place of each share is chosen by lot. No one from the first count is left except Caleb and Joshua.

They ask for land among their father’s brothers so his name is not lost. Moses brings their case to the LORD. The LORD says the daughters are right and must receive the inheritance. He makes it a rule: with no son, the land goes to a daughter. Then the LORD tells Moses he will see the land and die. Moses asks for a new leader and lays hands on Joshua before the people.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD tells Israel to bring his offerings at their set times. Two lambs are offered every day, one in the morning and one at evening. Each comes with flour, oil, and a drink offering. Two more lambs are offered every Sabbath. At each new month there are bulls, a ram, and seven lambs. Passover is on the fourteenth day of the first month. Seven days of unleavened bread follow, with offerings each day. The feast of weeks has its own offerings.

chapterMaps.narrative: The seventh month has three sacred times. The first day is a day of trumpets with rest and offerings. The tenth day is a day to humble oneself and do no work. On the fifteenth day a seven-day feast begins. Thirteen bulls are offered the first day, and one fewer each day after. On the seventh day there are seven bulls. The eighth day is a solemn assembly with one bull. These offerings are in addition to vows and free gifts.

chapterMaps.narrative: Moses tells the tribal heads the LORD’s rule on vows. A man who vows must not break his word. A young woman’s vow stands if her father hears it and says nothing. If he forbids it that day, it does not stand, and the LORD forgives her. A wife’s vow stands if her husband hears and says nothing. If he forbids it that day, it is void. A widow’s or divorced woman’s vow stands. A husband who cancels a vow later bears her guilt.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD tells Moses to take vengeance on Midian before he dies. Twelve thousand men go to war with Phinehas the priest. They kill Midian’s men, its five kings, and Balaam. They bring back the women, children, and herds. Moses is angry that the women were spared, because of what happened at Peor. He orders the boys and the women who have lain with a man killed. The soldiers purify themselves seven days outside the camp. The plunder is divided, and the officers give gold because no soldier was lost.

chapterMaps.narrative: Reuben and Gad have large herds and want the grazing land east of the Jordan. They ask Moses for it and ask not to cross the river. Moses asks if their brothers should go to war while they sit there. He says they are acting like the spies who discouraged Israel. They promise to build towns for their families and then fight in front of Israel. They will not go home until every tribe has its land. Moses agrees and warns that their sin will find them out if they fail. He gives them and half of Manasseh the lands of Sihon and Og.

Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh already have land east of the Jordan. Eleazar the priest and Joshua will divide the land. One leader from each tribe is named to help, with Caleb for Judah.

chapterMaps.narrative: Israel must give the Levites forty-eight towns with pasture land around them. Six of these are cities of refuge. A person who kills someone by accident may flee there from the avenger. He must not die before he stands trial before the community. One who killed with a weapon or from hatred is put to death. One who killed without hatred stays in the city until the high priest dies. No one is put to death on one witness alone. No payment can free a murderer, because blood pollutes the land.

chapterMaps.narrative: The family heads of Manasseh come to Moses with a problem. Zelophehad’s daughters will inherit land. If they marry men of another tribe, the land will pass to that tribe. Moses answers by the LORD’s word that they speak rightly. The daughters may marry whom they think best, but only within their father’s tribe. Any daughter who inherits land must do the same. The five daughters marry sons of their father’s brothers. So their land stays in Manasseh, and the book ends in the plains of Moab.

textRoutes.title: The journey remembered
textRoutes.summary: Moses writes down the stages of Israel’s journey at the LORD’s command. The list begins at Rameses, the day after the Passover. Egypt is burying its firstborn as Israel leaves. Dozens of camps are named, from the Red Sea to Sinai to Kadesh. Aaron dies on Mount Hor in the fortieth year, at age 123. The list ends in the plains of Moab by the Jordan. The LORD tells Israel to drive out Canaan’s people and destroy their idols. Any who remain will be like thorns in Israel’s sides.
textRoutes.detail: Verse 2 says Moses wrote these stages “by the commandment of the LORD.” So the record itself is commanded, not only the travel. Most of the entries are just two verbs: they traveled, they camped. A few stop for a memory: the Passover night, Elim’s water, Aaron’s death. The list includes the hard places with the good ones. Forty years of wandering become a line a reader can follow. It ends at the Jordan, with orders for the next step (verses 50–53).
